title.en: Show the constraint, not just the movement

summary: Encode waiting, utilisation and starvation directly, because moving objects alone hide where a process is limited.
objective: Compose an operational scene around the question the viewer actually has: what limits this system.
applies_when: A process scene is meant to explain performance rather than to decorate.
Several stations, lanes or resources operate at different rates.
A user asks what to change to make the process faster.
example_prompts: Make it obvious which station is holding up the line.
Show which pickers are idle and which are overloaded.
negative_signals: Scenes intended purely as atmosphere, such as a busy factory backdrop.
Single-resource processes where the constraint is not in question.
not_for: Scenes intended purely as atmosphere, such as a busy factory backdrop.
Single-resource processes where the constraint is not in question.

principles: Motion is a poor encoder of performance. A fast conveyor and a slow one look similar in a short clip, while a growing buffer in front of a station is unmistakable.
The informative quantities are accumulations and idleness: work waiting, resources idle, and time blocked. These are the direct evidence of a constraint.
A bottleneck is a system property, not a station property. It moves when the mix or the capacity changes, so the display should be able to show it moving.
Adding more moving objects to convey busyness usually reduces legibility; adding one honest accumulation usually increases it.
implementation: Give every station a visible buffer whose length is the real queue, so accumulation is spatially legible rather than a number in a corner.
Encode resource state with a persistent channel such as colour or a status band: idle, working, blocked, down.
Include a compact time series or sparkline of queue length or utilisation, since a bottleneck is a pattern over time rather than a single frame.
Give the viewer a control that changes one capacity and let them watch the constraint move, which teaches more than a static label.
Keep the framing wide enough that the accumulation and the affected stations are visible together.
observable_checks: Pause at a random moment and ask which station is limiting, then check the answer against the model. Reading a queue length, a utilisation figure or a sparkline is a legitimate way to answer; what fails the check is an encoding that supports no correct answer, or one whose visual impression contradicts the underlying numbers.

Increase capacity at the labelled bottleneck and compare the result against the declared network model: the accumulation should move to the next binding constraint, or clear entirely when demand is below every remaining station's capacity. A backlog that simply disappears is the correct outcome in that case, not a missing bottleneck.
Check that idle and blocked states are distinguishable, since both look like a stopped machine.
Confirm the buffer visualisation is bounded and readable when the queue becomes very long.

creative_affordances: Abstract or metaphorical encodings such as water levels or pressure gauges are welcome when the mapping is explained.
A stylised factory can carry accurate flow information; legibility does not require a chart aesthetic.
known_limits: Authored composition guidance; it makes no performance claim about any real facility and no runtime scene was inspected.
Identifying the true constraint still requires a valid model of the process.
